methods.text:

Sow singly in small pots or modules. Pot on if the roots fill the container. Harden off before planting outside.

Sow outside 

Sow in warm soil after frost. Leave one plant per compost-rich pocket. Bush and trailing types need different spacings.

Plant out 

Set the whole rootball into the pocket and water well. Use fleece on cold nights while plants settle. Remove covers as flowering starts so insects can reach the flowers.

text:
Squashes and Pumpkins.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Pick summer squash young and tender. Leave winter squash and pumpkins on the plant to develop sweet flesh and hard skins for storage.

Quick facts
Sow indoors

Apr–May. Start winter types early.

Harvest

Jul – Oct

Germination

5–8 days

Per station

One plant.

Sow

Late May–early Jun, after frost.

Plant out

Late May–Jun, after frost.

Sowing depth

Indoors: squash 5/8 in., pumpkins about 1/2 in.; outdoors: 1 in.

Each way

Bush 3 ft, trailing 5 ft, giants 6½ ft or more. Check the variety.

Yield per plant

Squash: several summer fruits or a few mature winter ones. Pumpkins: 1–3, fewer for giants.

Ready in

Summer 8–12; winter 16–24 weeks from sowing

Recommended varieties
WINTER SQUASH
Crown Prince F1

Blue-grey winter squash with rich orange flesh. Stores well for roasting and winter meals.

WINTER SQUASH
Uchiki Kuri

Red-orange winter squash with manageable fruits and rich flesh for cooking and autumn storage.

WINTER SQUASH
Hunter F1

Pale-tan butternut with orange flesh for autumn harvests and winter meals.

WINTER SQUASH
Sweet Dumpling

Small, striped winter squash for individual portions, alongside larger storage types.

PUMPKIN
Jack O'Lantern

Orange pumpkin mainly for Halloween carving. Give trailing stems room.

Key risks
Slugs

Slugs attack seedlings and young plants, especially in cold wet conditions, and may damage fruit resting on the soil.

Mildew

Powdery mildew produces a white coating on leaves, often late in the season.

Stem damage and rot

A broken stalk or damaged skin provides an entry point for storage rot.

No fruit

Poor pollination can leave flowers without developing fruit, especially in cool weather.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
86
FRUITING CROPS

Give storage squash a full season.

Smaller, quicker varieties ripen more reliably in cool gardens.

Keep the stalk intact at harvest.

A broken stalk invites rot; carry the fruit from underneath.

Soil & preparation
Warmest sunny, sheltered site; rich, moist, drained soil. Compost each planting station.
Allow room to trail; pumpkin stems root at nodes in bare, moist soil. Smaller varieties suit short seasons.
Sowing & planting
Start in a pot
Give room to spread
Sow in pots 

Sow singly in small pots or modules. Pot on if the roots fill the container. Harden off before planting outside.

Sow outside 

Sow in warm soil after frost. Leave one plant per compost-rich pocket. Bush and trailing types need different spacings.

Plant out 

Set the whole rootball into the pocket and water well. Use fleece on cold nights while plants settle. Remove covers as flowering starts so insects can reach the flowers.

Looking after the crop
Water at planting and as fruit swells, especially in dry weather. Mulch and weed before foliage covers the ground.
Let insects reach flowers; hand-pollinate if needed. Strong eating types: several fruits; giant show pumpkins: one. Rest fruit on tiles/boards off wet soil.
Harvesting & storage
Pick summer squash young. Cut winter fruit before frost, once skins harden and stalks turn corky.
Leave about 4 in. of sound stalk. Cure ripe fruit in sun 1–2 weeks; bring under cover for frost/rain. Store dry, airy and apart at 50–59°F; check soft patches. Use sound unripe fruit promptly. Never carry by stalks: breaks admit rot.
Discard unusually bitter or rotten fruit. Keep eating pumpkins separate from carved outdoor displays.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Young plants or low fruit are chewed.	Inspect and hand-pick; protect establishment.
Mildew	White powder develops on leaves.	Keep roots moist; late attacks matter less near ripeness.
Stem damage and rot	Rot enters around a broken stalk.	Cut with stalk intact; never lift fruit by it.
No fruit	Flowers fail to set useful fruit.	Allow insect access; hand-pollinate where needed.
Soft underripe fruit	Skins stay soft.	Use sound fruit promptly. Try an earlier variety.
Ground rot	Fruit softens against damp soil.	Raise on a clean board or tile; remove rotten fruit.
Bitterness	Fruit tastes unusually bitter.	Discard bitter fruit; cooking does not make it safe.
Cucumber mosaic virus	Mottled, distorted leaves. Weak plants.	Remove infected plants; monitor aphids and clear weed hosts.
Final tips

Never carry squash or pumpkins by their stalks; support the weight of the fruit.

Inspect stored fruit regularly and remove any showing soft patches or rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 117–121 · Growing Techniques 150
87
